big: ₹10,000 a month for 20 years at an assumed 12% a year grows to about ₹1 crore. Raise the SIP 10% each year and it nearly doubles. Show both, and say plainly which parts are assumptions.

lines: I started a ₹10,000 SIP at 30. How much will I have at 50?
At an assumed 12% a year, about a crore. Now watch what a yearly step-up does to that number, and what it costs her.

alt: Twenty bars of monthly instalments rising 10 percent each year against a dashed flat 10,000 rupee outline
caps: Meena starts at ₹10,000 a month and raises it 10% each year as her salary grows.
Year 5: ₹14,641 a month. The dashed outlines show the flat ₹10,000 she would otherwise pay.
By year 20 the instalment is ₹61,159 a month.
At an assumed 12% a year, the flat SIP reaches about ₹1 crore. The step-up reaches about ₹1.99 crore.

h: Bigger plan, not a better return
alt: Bars comparing money put in, final corpus and growth for a step-up SIP and a flat SIP over twenty years
caps: Same 12% a year, same 20 years. The step-up puts in ₹68.7 lakh, against ₹24 lakh for the flat SIP.
The corpus is about twice as big: ₹1.99 crore against ₹1 crore.
Each ₹1 put in became ₹2.89 with the step-up and ₹4.16 flat. Later money has less time to grow.
Step-up is a bigger plan, not a higher return. Both earn the same 12% a year.
rows: Growth on top of it (₹ lakh)

alt: Bars showing years to double at 6, 8, 9, 12 and 18 percent a year using the rule of 72
caps: Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly return to get the years money takes to double.
At 6% money doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, in about 8.
At 12%, in 6 years, and again in the next 6: ₹10,000 becomes ₹40,000.
Handy in a client chat. It is close for 6 to 12%, a little rough above that.

h: What if the return is lower?
intro: The same two SIPs over 20 years at different assumed returns.
note: Assumed returns are not promises. A four-point lower return cuts the flat corpus by about 41%, so show the range.

q: Meena's ₹5 lakh grows at an assumed 9% a year. By the Rule of 72, in about how many years could it reach ₹20 lakh?
why: At 9% the rule gives 72 divided by 9, which is 8 years, but that is one doubling only, to ₹10 lakh.
Twelve years is one doubling at 6%, not 9%. It also stops at ₹10 lakh, short of the target.
Each doubling takes 8 years at 9%. ₹5 lakh becomes ₹10 lakh, then ₹20 lakh: two doublings, about 16 years.
Twenty-four years is three doublings, which would reach ₹40 lakh. The target needs only two.

q: A client says a ₹10,000 step-up SIP and a flat ₹20,000 SIP both reach about ₹2 crore in 20 years at 12%, so they are the same plan. What should you point out?
opts: Flat needs ₹20,000 now and puts in ₹48 lakh; step-up ₹69 lakh
They are equal, since both end with about the same corpus
The step-up earns a higher rate, so it needs less money
The flat SIP always wins because its first instalment is bigger
why: The flat SIP puts in less in total but demands ₹20,000 from day one. The step-up starts small and puts in more over time.
The corpus matches, but the paths differ. One strains the budget early, the other later, and total money in is not equal.
Both earn the same 12% by assumption. The step-up reaches the corpus by putting in more money, not by earning more on it.
Flat does need less in total here, but a bigger first instalment is not always affordable, and a SIP that is dropped wins nothing.

q: After seeing ₹1 crore, Meena asks: "So I will have that?" If her fund earns 8% a year, not 12%, about what will her flat ₹10,000 SIP reach in 20 years?
opts: About ₹80 lakh, a fifth below ₹1 crore
About ₹24 lakh, just what she invested
why: Scaling by 8 over 12 is tempting, but compounding makes the shortfall larger than the drop in the rate suggests.
At 8% the 20-year corpus is about ₹59.3 lakh, 41% lower than at 12%. A small change in return moves the result a lot.
A fifth lower understates the effect. Over 20 years a four-point change in return compounds into a far larger gap.
₹24 lakh is her total investment. At 8% her money still grows, so the corpus is well above what she paid in.

q: A client's salary rises about 5% a year and a 10% step-up feels too steep. What is the best advice?
opts: Skip the step-up, since only 10% or more is worth doing
Step up 10% now and cut it back if money gets tight
Keep the SIP flat and add a lump sum later instead
Use 5%, which lifts the corpus to about ₹1.37 crore
why: Any step-up helps. A 5% step-up lifts ₹99.9 lakh to about ₹137 lakh, so the all-or-nothing view leaves value on the table.
A step-up she cannot keep up risks a stopped SIP, which is worse than a smaller rise she can sustain every year.
A later lump sum is rarely kept, and later money has less time to grow. A modest yearly rise does the work steadily.
A step-up matched to her income is one she will keep. At 5%, the same ₹10,000 start reaches about ₹1.37 crore.

pts: ₹10,000 a month for 20 years at an assumed 12% is about ₹1 crore (₹24 lakh in). A 10% yearly step-up makes it about ₹1.99 crore (₹68.7 lakh in).
Step-up is a bigger plan, not a higher return. The return is an assumption: at 8% the flat SIP reaches about ₹59 lakh.
Rule of 72: years to double is about 72 divided by the yearly return.
